meta.title: Ice for July
meta.skill_frame: Text structure: follow a set of steps and see why each position has a reason.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 5.7, 5.2 and 5.7 on the three parts (114, 109 and 102 words), 5.5 together, near the band's floor. The load is a five-step seasonal chain in which each step has a reason of its own: snow insulates, scored lines guide the saw, sawdust slows heat, and the month decides how much ice there is. The reader has to hold four separate reasons and not collapse them into one.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.attribution: Original text drafted for text_structure 4.1, Band 4.1, sequence 1. No external work.
source.text_status: Drafted for the band, accepted on spot check.
source.survey: A historical trade with no single event: the sequence carries the lesson, and the closing part asks why the order could not be changed.
source.avoided: No town, company, price, or date. No claim about who bought the ice.

session.difficulty_basis: Each item names one reason for one position in the sequence; the last joins weather to yield.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: Before electric refrigeration reached small towns, a pond with thick ice was worth money. The work started in the coldest weeks of January, when the ice was thick enough to hold a horse. A crew scraped the snow off the pond with wide wooden blades. Snow blankets the ice and keeps it from growing, so the snow had to go first. Then the crew scored the surface in a grid with a saw, cutting shallow lines about two feet apart. Real cutting began only after that scoring. A straight line of cuts guided every later stroke. Each block was floated to a ramp at the shore and hauled up by a team of horses.
passage.part_2: The blocks did not go straight to a customer. They went first into an ice house, a windowless building with thick walls and no heat at all. Workers packed the blocks in sawdust and stacked them almost to the roof. Sawdust is a poor conductor of heat, so it slowed the melting to a trickle instead of a stream. The house was filled in January and opened for business in June. By then the outside of the stack had melted into a rough shell. A good house held a summer of ice for a town of a few thousand people. A block cut in winter could last until August.
passage.part_3: The order of the work could not be changed, and the reason was the weather. Ice cut in March is thinner and softer than ice cut in January, so the crew waited for the cold and not for the calendar. Packing came right after hauling, because a block left in the sun lost an inch on every side. The house had to stay shut all summer as well. A door left open on a warm day let in more melting air than a week of hauling could replace. A crew that cut in the wrong week wasted a whole season of work.

items.prompt: Why did the crew scrape the snow off the pond before they began to cut?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. Snow keeps the ice from growing thicker.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The second and third sentences say snow blankets the ice and keeps it from growing, so it had to go first.
tutor_only.tell: Snow works like a blanket over a pond. Under the snow the ice stops getting thicker, so the crew cleared it away first.
help: Find the sentence that begins 'Snow blankets the ice'.
It says what the snow does to the ice underneath.
tutor_only.core_idea: Snow keeps the ice from growing thicker.
accept_ideas: snow keeps the ice from thickening
the snow stops the ice from growing
snow insulates the ice and holds it back
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the ice was dirty
if_they_say.ask: Dirt is not the reason given. What does the passage say snow does to the ice?

items.prompt: Why did the crew score the surface before cutting all the way through?

tutor_only.confirm: Yes. A line of shallow cuts guided every later stroke.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says real cutting began only after the scoring, since a straight line of cuts guided every later stroke.
tutor_only.tell: The scored line is a guide. Once the saw has a straight groove to follow, every later cut stays where the crew wants it.
help: Read the sentence that begins 'Real cutting began only after'.
It says what the scored lines did for the saw.
tutor_only.core_idea: The scored lines guided every later cut.
accept_ideas: the shallow cuts kept the later cuts straight
it gave the saw a line to follow
not_required: how many workers scored the ice
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says scoring made the blocks lighter
if_they_say.ask: Lifting is a different job. What did the scored lines do for the cutting?

items.prompt: Why were the blocks packed in sawdust?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. Sawdust is a poor conductor of heat, so it slowed the melting.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says sawdust is a poor conductor of heat, so it slowed the melting to a trickle.
tutor_only.tell: Sawdust holds heat out. Packed around the blocks, it keeps them from melting as fast as they would in open air.
help: Look at the sentence about sawdust and heat.
It names what the sawdust did to the melting.
accept_ideas: it made the ice last longer
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says sawdust kept the blocks clean
if_they_say.ask: Cleaning is not the reason given. What does sawdust do to heat and melting?

items.prompt: The crew could have cut ice in March. Why did they wait for January?

tutor_only.confirm: Yes. March ice is thinner and softer than January ice.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says ice cut in March is thinner and softer than ice cut in January, so the crew waited for the cold.
tutor_only.tell: The same pond gives less ice as the winter ends. January ice is thick and hard. March ice is thin and soft. So the month decides how much work pays.
help: Read the first sentence of this part about March ice.
It compares March ice with January ice.
tutor_only.core_idea: The ice is thinner in March.
accept_ideas: the ice is thinner in March
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says January ice is cleaner
if_they_say.ask: Cleanliness is not the reason given. What happens to ice as the winter goes on?

tutor_only.full_idea: March ice is thinner and softer, so the crew waited for the cold.

items.prompt: The passage says a crew that cut in the wrong week wasted a season of work. What made the week matter so much?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The ice was thick only in the coldest weeks, so a late crew had less ice to cut.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The passage says the work started in the coldest weeks, that March ice is thinner and softer, and that the house was filled in January.
tutor_only.tell: The month decides the ice. Cut in the cold weeks and the blocks are thick. Cut later and there is less ice, and softer ice, for the same work.
help: Compare what the passage says about January with what it says about March.
The two months give ice of different thickness.
tutor_only.core_idea: The ice was thinner later in the year.
accept_ideas: the ice was thinner later in the year
the ice got soft as the weather warmed
they had to cut while the ice was thick
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the crew was too busy in March
if_they_say.ask: The passage gives a reason about the ice. What happens to ice as the winter ends?

if_they_say.when: the student says March had more snow
if_they_say.ask: More snow is what the crew scraped off. What does the passage say about the ice itself in March?

tutor_only.full_idea: The ice was thick in January and thin in March, so a late crew had less to cut.
